beats.say: Solve four to the power X, minus three times two to the power X, plus two, equals zero.
The plan: write everything with base two. Then it becomes a quadratic in two to the power X.
asks: What is a quadratic in disguise?

beats.say: The other term is two to the power X, so write four with base two: four is two squared.
So the equation becomes two squared to the power X, minus three times two to the power X, plus two, equals zero.
Times power: two squared to the power X is two to the power two X, which is two to the power X, all squared.
asks: Why can I swap the powers?

beats.say: Now the equation has two to the power X, and two to the power X, all squared. A quadratic in disguise.

do.on: two to the power X, and

beats.say: So substitute: let A equal two to the power X.
asks: Can I use u instead of a?

beats.say: Then two to the power X, all squared, becomes A squared, and three times two to the power X becomes three A.
asks: Where do a squared and 3a come from?

beats.say: So the equation becomes A squared minus three A plus two equals zero.
asks: Is this a normal quadratic now?

beats.say: Solve the quadratic: it factorises into A minus two, times A minus one.
So A equals two, or A equals one. Both are positive, as two to the power X always is.
Now bring back X. The question asks for X, so each value of A gives a value of X.
asks: Why can't I stop at a?

beats.say: A equals two: two to the power X is two, which is two to the power one.
asks: Why write 2 as 2 to the power 1?

do.on: two to the power X is two

beats.say: Since the base is the same, the powers must be the same: X equals one.
asks: Why can I compare the powers?

beats.say: A equals one: two to the power X is one, which is two to the power zero. So X equals zero.
asks: Why is 1 the same as 2 to the power 0?

do.on: two to the power X is one

beats.say: So X equals one, or X equals zero.
